δέον καὶ τὴν κτῆσιν τοῦ μακαρίου βίου ἀναλίσκων αὐτόν. ἐξαγοραζόμενοι δὲ τὸν
καιρὸν ὄντα ἐν ἡμέραις πονηραῖς οἱονεὶ μεταποιοῦμεν τὰς πονηρὰς ἡμέρας εἰς
ἀγαθάς, καὶ ὡσπερεὶ ἑαυτοῖς ποιοῦμεν αὐτὰς εἶναι οὐ τοῦ ἐνε τῶτο αἰῶνο ἡμέρας
πονηρὰ ἀλλὰ τοῦ μέλλοντο αἰῶνο ἡμέρας ἀγαθάς. 〚[v. 17] διὰ τοῦτο μὴ γίνεσθε
ἄφρονες ἀλλὰ συνιέντες τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Κυρίου. διὰ ποῖον τοῦτο, ἢ τὸ βλέπειν
ἀκριβῶς πῶς περιπατεῖτε μὴ ὡς ἄσοφοι ἀλλ' ὡς σοφοί, μὴ γίνεσθε ἄφρονες; εἰ γὰρ
ἔσεσθε ἄφρονες, ἀκριβῶς οὐ περιπατή σετε οὐδὲ ὡς σοφοί. προστάσσει δὲ αὐτοῖς τὸ
τοῦ Κυρίου ἐξετάζειν θέλημα καὶ συνιέναι αὐτό, ἵν' ὅπου τι περὶ τοῦ πράττειν
καταλάβοιεν, αὐτὸ πράττωσιν ὡς θέλημα Κυρίου, ὅπου δὲ πάσχ<ω>σι φέρ<ω>σιν
αὐτὸ ὡς θελήματι γινόμενον Κυρίου.〛 28 Eph. v18 καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ ἐν ᾧ
ἐστὶν ἀσωτία, ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι. [Ὠριγένης φησί] δύναται μὲν καὶ
ἁπλούστερον ταῦτα νοεῖσθαι, ἀσωτίας οὔσης ἐν τῇ χρήσει τοῦ μεθύειν ποιοῦντος
οἴνου. δύναται δὲ καὶ οἶνος ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν ἀσωτία νοεῖσθαι περὶ οὗ ἐν ᾠδῇ μεγάλῃ
λέγεται θυμὸ δρακόντων ὁ οἶνο αὐτῶν καὶ θυμὸ ἀ πίδων ἀνίατο , ὅντινα πάντες οἱ
ἐξιστάμενοι καὶ μεθύοντες τὸν λογισμὸν πίνουσι πολλὴν ἔχοντα τὴν ἀσωτίαν. πρὸς
ἀντιδιαστολὴν δὲ ἐκείνου τοῦ οἴνου τοῦ μεθύσκοντος ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν ἀσωτία ἐναντίος
νοεῖται ὁ πεπληρωμένος πνεύματι καὶ πᾶν ὃ χωρεῖ τοῦ θειοτέρου λαμβάνων.
πολλάκις δὲ τετηρήκαμεν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ «πνεύματος» χωρὶς προσθήκης γεγραμμένον
ὅτι ἐπὶ κρείττονος εἴρηται, ὅπερ καὶ ἐνθάδε σημαίνεται. 29 Eph. v19 [λαλοῦντες
ἑαυτοῖς ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ
καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ.] [Ὠριγένης δέ φησιν] οἱ μὲν ὕμνοι δύναμιν καὶ θειότητα
καταγγέλλουσι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ εἴη ἂν ὁ ἐπιστήμων τοῦ θεολογεῖν ἐν ὕμνοις
πνευματικοῖς· τάχα δὲ ὁ περὶ τῶν πρακτέων διαλαμβάνων καὶ τῶν οἷς δεῖ ἐνεργεῖν
διὰ τοῦ ὡς ψαλτηρίου ὀργάνου σωματικοῦ ἡμῶν, οὗτος ἐν ψαλμοῖς ἐστι
πνευματικοῖς· ὁ δὲ ἄλλως φυσιολογῶν περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου τάξεως καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν
δημιουργημάτων, οὗτος ἐν ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς. καὶ χρή γε ᾄδειν κατὰ τὴν
φυσιολογίαν καὶ ψάλλειν κατὰ τὴν περὶ τῶν ἠθῶν διέξοδον τῷ Κυρίῳ διακείμενον
γνησίως πρὸς τὰ λεγόμενα· τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ ψάλλειν καὶ ᾄδειν τῇ καρδίᾳ τῷ
Κυρίῳ. [v 20] εὐχαριστοῦντες πάντοτε ὑπὲρ πάντων ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν

πάντοτε χαίρετε ἀδιαλείπτω προ εύχε θε ἐν παντὶ εὐχαρι τεῖτε. ταύτην δὴ τηρήσει
τὴν ἐντολὴν ὁ διειληφὼς περὶ τῆς προνοίας φθανούσης καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ βʹ ἀ αρίων
πωλούμενα πέντε τρουθία ὧν ἓν οὐ πίπτει εἰ παγίδα χωρὶ τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖ πατρό .
τὸ δὲ ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖν καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων εὐχαριστεῖν ἐστιν· οὐκοῦν καὶ ἐπὶ ταῖς
περιστάσεσιν εὐχαριστητέον, ἐπείπερ καὶ αὗται τῶν ἐφ' οἷς δεῖ εὐχαριστεῖν εἰσιν· καὶ
ὥσπερ δεῖ εὐχαριστεῖν τὸν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐν τῷ μεταλαμ βάνειν τοῦ κόσμου καὶ
καταθεᾶσθαι τὸ κάλλος αὐτοῦ καὶ θεωρεῖν
pass_a_gloss: needful and spending it on the acquisition of the blessed life. And redeeming the time that is in evil days we as it were remake the evil days into good, and as it were make them for ourselves not days of the present age that are evil but days of the coming age that are good. Therefore do not become foolish but understanding what the will of the Lord is. Because of what this? Or because of looking carefully how you walk not as unwise but as wise, do not become foolish? For if you will be foolish, you will not walk carefully nor as wise. And he commands them to examine the Lord's will and understand it, so that wherever they grasp something about acting they may do it as the Lord's will, and wherever they suffer they may bear it as coming about by the Lord's will. And do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in spirit. Origen says: these can also be understood more simply, debauchery being in the use of wine that makes drunk. And wine in which is debauchery can also be understood about that of which in the great song it is said the wine of dragons is their wrath and incurable wrath of asps, which all who are beside themselves and drunk in reasoning drink, having much debauchery. And in contrast to that wine that makes drunk in which is debauchery, the opposite is understood as the one filled with spirit and taking all of the more divine that he has room for. And we have often observed the name spirit written without addition that it is said upon the better, which is also signified here. Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord. Origen says: hymns announce power and divinity of God, and the one skilled in theologizing would be in spiritual hymns; and perhaps the one treating of things to be done and of those with which one must act through our bodily organ as a psaltery is in spiritual psalms; and the one otherwise doing natural philosophy about the order of the world and the other created things is in spiritual songs. And one must sing according to natural philosophy and make melody according to the exposition about morals to the Lord, being disposed genuinely toward the things said; for this is to make melody and sing with the heart to the Lord. Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and Father. And in the first to the Thessalonians he says always rejoice, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks. This commandment the one who has grasped about providence reaching even to the two sparrows sold for a penny, of which one does not fall into a snare apart from the Father in heaven, will keep. And to give thanks in everything is also to give thanks for all things; therefore one must give thanks also in circumstances, since these too are among the things for which one must give thanks; and just as one must give thanks while in the world in partaking of the world and contemplating its beauty and beholding how many and of what sort of things have come about because of the rational, so also one must give thanks upon the things in part. And the one giving thanks to God and Father must give thanks in the mediator of God and humans, so that we do the giving thanks to God and Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Submitting, he says, to one another in the fear of Christ. This is very destructive of being fond of rule and fond of being first. For this commandment is given to all, for being free from all I enslaved myself to all that I might gain all. And also the commandment saying Serve one another commands this. Therefore through love the apostles served the churches, ministering and assisting the salvation of humans. And the Savior himself took the form of a slave not so much for any other reason as for having served the disciples, so that also once putting water into the basin he washed the disciples' feet. And also the one who understands The one wanting to be great among you will be slave of all submits according to serving those whom one must. Yet it is possible that the one serving, doing in the serving what is suitable for those served, seem not to submit, when contrary to not knowing what is advantageous those served order those willing to serve to do things not fitting for them. Yet even then the one doing toward the advantageous both serves and submits to the need of the one he serves, because of the passionless and beatifying fear according to the word of God. For this I think—
pass_b_english: —needful, spending time on gaining the blessed life. By redeeming time in evil days we remake those days into good, and make them for ourselves not evil days of the present age but good days of the age to come.

[[Ephesians 5:17 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:17]] "Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the Lord's will is." Why "therefore"? Because you look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise—so do not become foolish. Fools will not walk carefully or wisely. Examine the Lord's will and grasp it: where you see what to do, do it as his will; where you suffer, bear it as coming by his will.

[[Ephesians 5:18 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:18]] "And do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in spirit." Simply, debauchery sits in drunken use of wine. There is also the wine of the great song—"their wine is the wrath of dragons, and the incurable wrath of asps"—which all who are beside themselves and drunk in reasoning drink, full of debauchery. Against that wine stands the one filled with spirit, taking all of the more divine he can hold. We have often noted "spirit" without addition said of the better; so here too.

[[Ephesians 5:19 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:19]] "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." Hymns announce God's power and divinity; the skilled theologian lives in spiritual hymns. The one treating deeds and what must be done through our bodily instrument as a psaltery is in spiritual psalms. The one philosophizing nature—the world's order and other created things—is in spiritual songs. Sing according to that natural study and make melody according to moral exposition, truly disposed toward what is said: that is singing and making melody with the heart to the Lord.

[[Ephesians 5:20 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:20]] "Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and Father." Compare 1 Thessalonians: always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. Keep this if you grasp providence that reaches even two sparrows sold for a penny, of which none falls apart from the Father. To give thanks in everything is to give thanks for all things—including hard circumstances. As one thanks God while sharing the world's beauty and seeing what was made for the rational creature, so also for particular things. Thank God and Father in the mediator of God and humans—in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[[Ephesians 5:21 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:21]] "Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ." This pulls down love of rule and of being first. The command is for all: "Free from all, I enslaved myself to all that I might gain all," and "Serve one another." Through love the apostles served the churches for human salvation. The Savior took a slave's form chiefly to serve the disciples—even putting water in the basin and washing their feet. Whoever understands "the one wanting to be great among you will be slave of all" submits by serving those who must be served.

A servant doing what suits those served may seem not to submit when the served, not knowing what helps them, order unfit things. Even then the one who acts for what truly helps both serves and submits to that need, because of passionless, beatifying fear according to God's word. That fear, I think, is what "in the fear of Christ" shows—continued next.
